factual_errors.claim: 'Verify power and link status -- with the PLC locked out and de-energized, confirm the converter is powered and its LEDs show a live RS-485 link.'
factual_errors.why_wrong: This is internally contradictory: you cannot confirm a device 'is powered' or observe 'live' link LEDs while the equipment is locked out and de-energized. As written this instruction can't actually be executed, and a technician trying to follow it literally would either skip the check or re-energize without realizing the wording assumed otherwise.

factual_errors.claim: No warning about DH-485 0-5V RS-485 levels vs. Ethernet voltages
factual_errors.why_wrong: This is the exact scenario (swapping in an Ethernet-side converter on a DH-485 RJ45 port) where wiring a standard Ethernet device into the port risks damaging the network card or PLC processor. The answer never raises this, despite it being flagged as a critical gap in the prior grading round for this identical question.

notes: Answer is honestly labelled as general reasoning (answer_basis=general_reasoning, no fabricated citations) and correctly identifies the high-level root cause -- a real improvement in evidence honesty over the 09-05 version, which asserted specific advice with zero grounding and no disclosure. But the diagnostic sequence contains a self-contradictory instruction (checking a de-energized device for live LEDs/power status), it never names the documented replacement interfaces (1747-AIC, 1761-NET-AIC) as the definitive fix, omits TX-EN/token-passing arbitration, and -- again -- omits the 0-5V vs. Ethernet voltage damage risk that this specific swap makes directly relevant. Correctness and safety both fall short of the bar.
